title: Windows and Order
focus: Week two opens with the three patterns that show up most often in a real Google phone screen.

cards.title: Variable Sliding Window
cards.trigger: Longest or shortest contiguous run satisfying a condition, on non-negative or set-like data.
cards.recall: Write longest-substring-without-repeats from memory. Then answer: the shrink is a `while`, not an `if`. When does that matter, and what problem shape makes `if` sufficient?
useWhen: Longest substring with at most k distinct characters
Longest substring without repeating characters
Minimum window containing all of a target multiset
Smallest subarray with sum at least k, non-negative values only
Longest repeating character replacement
template: # LONGEST: shrink only while the window is invalid
if ch in last and last[ch] >= left:
left = last[ch] + 1     # jump, do not crawl
# SHORTEST: shrink while the window is still VALID, recording as you go
keyInsights: Longest shrinks while INVALID. Shortest shrinks while VALID. Getting these backwards is the number one sliding-window bug
`last[ch] >= left` is required, otherwise a stale index outside the window drags `left` backwards
Sliding window requires that extending the window only ever moves the metric one way. Negative numbers break that, use prefix sums instead
cards.trap: 'The array has negative numbers.' The window is no longer monotonic and sliding window is simply wrong. Say so and switch to prefix sum with a map.

cards.title: Linked List Surgery
cards.trigger: Pointer rewiring where you must not lose the rest of the list.
cards.recall: Write the iterative reversal from memory. Then answer: there are exactly three pointers and the order of the four assignments matters. Say why saving `nxt` first is not optional.
useWhen: Reverse a whole list, or a sublist, or in groups of k
Merge two sorted lists, dummy head removes every edge case
Remove the nth node from the end, two pointers n apart
Detect a cycle and find its entry point
Reorder, palindrome check, split in half
template: # Reversal: save, point back, advance both
nxt = cur.next        # 1. save the rest of the list
# Dummy head: makes 'delete the first node' the same code as any other
# slow is now the middle; if slow is fast, restart one at head and step both by 1
keyInsights: Without saving `nxt` first you overwrite `cur.next` and the remainder of the list is unreachable
A dummy head eliminates every 'what if it is the head' branch. Use one by default, not as a rescue
Floyd's cycle entry works because the meeting point is exactly (cycle length minus offset) from the entry. Be ready to sketch that
cards.trap: 'Reverse only nodes m through n, in one pass.' You need the node before m held aside. People who only memorised full reversal stall here.

cards.title: BFS Variants
patterns: Right side view is last per level
cards.trigger: The question is about levels, or about what you would see from one side.
cards.recall: Write zigzag level order from memory. Then answer: is it cheaper to reverse the level list, or to append-left into a deque, and does either change the complexity?
useWhen: Level order, zigzag, bottom-up level order
Right or left side view
Average, max or sum per level
Minimum depth, BFS finds it faster than DFS on a wide tree
Largest value in each row, and level-wise connections
template: for _ in range(len(q)):            # snapshot the level size
# Right side view: just take the last node of every level
# Minimum depth: return the instant you pop a leaf

problem.name: Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal

keyInsights: Never reverse the queue itself. Reverse the output list for that level, or build it with appendleft
BFS space is O(width), which for a complete tree is n/2. DFS space is O(height). They are not interchangeable on space
Minimum depth via BFS exits at the first leaf. DFS must explore everything. Say that when they ask which you would use
cards.trap: 'Right side view, but the tree is a left-skewed chain.' The rightmost node per level is still the only node. If you special-cased 'take node.right' you are wrong.

cards.title: Unbounded Knapsack
cards.trigger: A supply of item types you may reuse freely, and a target to hit exactly or minimally.
cards.recall: Write coin change minimum from memory. Then answer both halves of the loop-order question: why forwards for capacity, and why does swapping the outer and inner loops change combinations into permutations?
useWhen: Fewest coins to make an amount
Number of ways to make an amount, order does not matter
Rod cutting and any repeat-allowed value maximisation
Perfect squares summing to n
Combination sum where reuse is allowed
template: # Minimum count: dp[a] = fewest coins summing to exactly a
return -1 if dp[amount] == INF else dp[amount]
# COUNT COMBINATIONS ({1,2} once):  coin outer, amount inner
# COUNT PERMUTATIONS ({1,2} and {2,1}): amount outer, coin inner
if c <= a: dp[a] += dp[a - c]
keyInsights: Forwards means `dp[a - c]` may already include coin c, which is exactly what unlimited reuse means
Coin outer counts combinations. Amount outer counts permutations. This is the most commonly botched detail in all of DP
Use `amount + 1` as infinity so `min` works and the unreachable check stays clean
cards.trap: 'Greedy: always take the largest coin.' Fails on coins [1,3,4] with amount 6, greedy gives 3, the answer is 2. Have that counterexample ready.

cards.title: Topological Sort
cards.trigger: Directed dependencies, and you must order them, or just prove an order exists.
cards.recall: Write Kahn's algorithm from memory. Then answer: how does this detect a cycle without any extra bookkeeping, and what exactly does the final count comparison mean?
useWhen: Course schedule, build order, task dependency resolution
Detect a cycle in a directed graph
Alien dictionary, derive an alphabet from ordered words
Longest path in a DAG, process in topological order
Parallel job scheduling, the number of rounds is the DAG height
template: def topo(n, edges):                    # edges are (prereq -> course)
q = deque(i for i in range(n) if indeg[i] == 0)
return order if len(order) == n else []   # short = cycle
# Hitting a GREY node is a back edge, which is a cycle.
keyInsights: Nodes inside a cycle never reach in-degree zero, so they are never emitted. The count check is the cycle test, free
Get the edge direction right. Prerequisite points to dependent. Reversing it silently produces a reversed order
Draining the queue level by level gives the minimum number of parallel rounds, a very common follow-up
cards.trap: 'Is the topological order unique?' Only if the queue never holds two nodes at once. Answering that shows you understand what the algorithm is really doing.
